# Study Overview

## Project Objective and Policy Impact

\justifying

- Estimate national-scale health impacts of dietary sodium reduction policies using a population CVD model.
- Quantify deaths and cases of ischemic heart disease (IHD), stroke, and hypertensive heart disease, as well as DALYs averted over 2026--2050.
- Conduct a full economic benefit--cost analysis to support government decision-making.
- Focus on RTSL partner countries and on policies that governments can realistically implement.

## Agenda for Today's Call

\footnotesize

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Walk through the 6 interventions} in the Sodium Lives Saved Calculator --- confirm effect sizes and source assignments.
    \item \textbf{Matti (if present)} discuss discretionary-vs-packaged disaggregation approach --- GDP regression, floor/ceiling values, BP effects of K and Na.
  \item \textbf{Decide pending items 1--4}: LSSS scenarios, mass media inclusion, observation-period harmonization, country-specific vs.\ regression-based sodium shares.
  \item \textbf{Lock revised timeline} for paper + report + Bloomberg renewal deliverable.
\end{enumerate}

# Recap of Prior Presentation

## Where We Left Off

\justifying
\footnotesize

- **Modeling framework**: Multi-state CVD life-table (Well $\to$ Sick $\to$ Dead) simulated annually over 2026--2050 for ages 20--95, four CVD causes (IHD, stroke, HHD, other CVD), by age $\times$ sex $\times$ country.
- **Outcome metrics**: Deaths averted, IHD/stroke/HHD cases averted, DALYs averted, plus full benefit--cost analysis (NPV, BCR).
- **Baseline scenario design**: Five SHAKE-aligned policy bundles with total sodium-reduction efficacy \texttt{salteff} ($\eta$) ranging from 0 (baseline) to 0.250 (full mandatory package).
- **Causal pathway**: Sodium $\to$ SBP (Filippini dose--response) $\to$ CVD incidence (Ettehad per-10-mmHg RRs) $\to$ life-table transitions.
- **Deliverables**: Peer-reviewed paper + RTSL report + interactive Shiny tool, originally targeted for end of June 2026 (per Apr 24 timeline).


## Sources of Sodium --- Current State

\justifying
\footnotesize

Zina and Nicole have been compiling literature on sodium shares across three categories:

\medskip
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Packaged foods}: Processed and ultra-processed sources, including salt-based condiments (fish sauce, soy sauce) where separately reported.
  \item \textbf{Discretionary sources}: Salt or MSG added while cooking at home or at the table.
  \item \textbf{Outside-the-home}: Restaurants, cafeterias/canteens, street food. Approximately $\frac{1}{3}$ of outside-home assumed to be institutional (public food procurement).
\end{itemize}

\medskip
This compilation feeds directly into the \textbf{Sodium Lives Saved Calculator} (next section) and determines how intervention effects are attributed to the correct sodium source.

\medskip
\textbf{Key method}: Where country-specific data are unavailable, discretionary share is predicted from GDP per capita using the Bhat/Marklund regression \autocite{marklund2022sources}. Processed share is predicted from discretionary share. Floors: 10\% discretionary (USA), 2\% packaged (Ethiopia).

# Sodium Lives Saved Calculator

## Calculator Overview

\justifying
\scriptsize

\textbf{Purpose}: Estimate national-scale lives saved from a portfolio of sodium-reducing interventions.

\textbf{Six intervention areas}: (A) Public food procurement, (B) Behavior change / mass media, (C) Low-sodium salt substitutes, (D) Front-of-pack labeling, (E) Mandatory salt targets, (F) Fiscal policy / taxation.

\textbf{Source disaggregation}: Sodium intake split into discretionary, packaged, and outside-the-home (with $\sim\!\frac{1}{3}$ of outside-home = institutional). Each intervention acts on its target source.

\textbf{Multiplicative combination}: Effects within a source are combined multiplicatively, not additively, to prevent ${>}$100\% reductions. E.g., tax (13.7\%) + FOPL (15\%) on packaged $\Rightarrow$ $1-(1-0.137)(1-0.15)=26.6\%$.

\textbf{Discretionary share}: Predicted from GDP per capita \autocite{marklund2022sources}; floors at 10\% (USA) and 2\% packaged (Ethiopia).

\textbf{Packaged-food growth}: Projected using Vandevijvere et al.\ 2019 regional growth rates \autocite{vandevijvere2019}, capped at Singapore (4.3 g Na/day from packaged).

\textbf{Demo}: \url{https://dcp-uw.shinyapps.io/salt_demo/} \quad \textbf{Code}: \url{https://github.com/Disease-Control-Priorities/sodium}

## Low-Sodium Salt Substitutes (LSSS)

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Discretionary salt.

\textbf{Study}: \textcite{huang2026} --- preprint (Matti et.al). Five scenarios:

\scriptsize
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Worldwide replacement of \textbf{all salt} (discretionary + non-discretionary)$^{a,b}$
  \item Worldwide replacement of \textbf{discretionary salt only}$^{a,b}$
  \item Worldwide replacement of non-discretionary salt only$^{a,b}$
  \item Replacement of discretionary salt for people with \textbf{diagnosed} hypertension$^{a,c}$
  \item Replacement of discretionary salt for people with \textbf{treated} hypertension$^{a,c}$
\end{enumerate}
\footnotesize
$^a$ Modeled BP-lowering benefits. $^b$ Includes hyperkalemia harms in CKD G3--G5. $^c$ Assumes clinical screening prevents use in 20\% of CKD G3--G5.

\medskip
\textbf{Working decision}: Focus on scenarios \textbf{4, 5} (discretionary-only). Pending confirmation.

## SHAKE 2.0 / Revamped SHAKE Package

\justifying
\footnotesize

The WHO SHAKE package (2026 revision) now incorporates \textbf{low-sodium salt substitutes} alongside the original five pillars:

\medskip
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{S}urveillance --- population sodium monitoring
  \item \textbf{H}arness Industry --- food reformulation (mandatory/voluntary targets)
  \item \textbf{A}dopt Standards --- front-of-pack labeling, marketing restrictions
  \item \textbf{K}nowledge --- consumer information and education campaigns
  \item \textbf{E}nvironments --- healthier food settings (institutional procurement)
  \item[\textbf{+}] \textbf{Low-Sodium Salt Substitutes (LSSS)} --- newly added to the SHAKE package, reflecting the WHO guideline on LSSS and growing trial evidence
\end{enumerate}

\medskip
The largest and most sustained sodium reductions occur when SHAKE components are implemented as a \textbf{package}. Our modeling evaluates individual and combined policy bundles mapped to these components, now including LSSS as a sixth intervention lever.

# Team Discussion

## Pending Decisions

\scriptsize

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{LSSS scenarios} --- Confirm we model scenarios 4 and 5 (discretionary-only: all adults / diagnosed HTN / treated HTN).
  \item \textbf{Mass media} --- In or out? Laura: RTSL funds policy change, not media for behavior change. SHAKE framing argues for inclusion in the paper; reinvestment case argues for exclusion.
  \item \textbf{Heterogeneity of observation periods} --- Effect sizes measured over very different time windows (1 yr $\to$ 20 yrs). How do we harmonize? Options: (a) assume effects are end-state, apply at full scale-up; (b) apply linearly over observed window; (c) use a country-tier heuristic (low/middle/high).
  \item \textbf{Source-of-sodium estimates} --- How hard do we push for country-specific shares vs.\ fall back on Marklund's GDP regression with floors/ceilings? Flag condiment-heavy countries where the packaged-food transition is escalating.
  \item \textbf{Integration with Matti's et.al} --- Confirm we use his discretionary-vs-GDP regression and BP-effect inputs; clarify co-authorship/coordination so we do not scoop the \emph{BMJ} paper.
    \item \textbf{Bloomberg renewal deliverable} --- What does the renewal application need from us, and by when, that is distinct from the paper?
  \item \textbf{Timeline} --- Original end-of-June paper submission is now +1--2 months for LSSS integration. New target?
\end{enumerate}

# Appendix

## A. Public Food Procurement

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Institutional share of outside-home consumption.

\textbf{Selected study}: \textcite{gase2011} --- modeling/simulation study, LA County.

\textbf{Policy simulated}: Two approaches --- (1) mandatory reformulation (reduce sodium content of all foods served); (2) choice architecture + incentives (labeling, promotion, subsidies, lower-Na alternatives).

\textbf{Effect size}: Weighted average across adult settings = \textbf{--233 mg/day ($\approx$7\%)} of 3,329 mg baseline. Applies only to settings where individuals eat $\geq$1 meal/day, $\geq$5 days/week, $\geq$8 weeks.

\textbf{Source-of-sodium adjustment}: 233 mg = 20.6\% reduction in sodium content of public meals. For a country where $x\%$ of sodium comes from institutional meals, population-level impact = $0.206 \times x\%$.

\textbf{Caveats}: Modeled, not observed; US-specific setting; very small affected population share.

<!-- \textbf{Population affected}: Only \textbf{0.176\%} of LA adult population (13,183 / 7,501,453). -->

## B. Behavior Change / Mass Media

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Discretionary + packaged.

\textbf{Candidate study 1}: \textcite{do2016} --- COMBI Vietnam. Multi-component intervention (mass media + school + community + high-risk targeting). \textbf{5\% decrease} in mean sodium excretion after 1-year intervention.

\textbf{Candidate study 2}: \textcite{collins2014} --- UK economic evaluation. Advertising campaign promoting healthy eating. \textbf{2\% [1--5\%]} effect size used in their model. Provenance of these numbers could not be verified in the source references.

\medskip

\begin{alertblock}{Open question}
Laura's noted that RTSL funds \textbf{policy change, not mass media for behavior change}. Should this intervention be included in the model? SHAKE framing argues for inclusion; reinvestment case argues for exclusion.
\end{alertblock}

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Discretionary salt.

\textbf{Study}: \textcite{huang2026} --- preprint (Marklund/TGI/Polly). Five scenarios:

\scriptsize
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Worldwide replacement of \textbf{all salt} (discretionary + non-discretionary)$^{a,b}$
  \item Worldwide replacement of \textbf{discretionary salt only}$^{a,b}$
  \item Worldwide replacement of non-discretionary salt only$^{a,b}$
  \item Replacement of discretionary salt for people with \textbf{diagnosed} hypertension$^{a,c}$
  \item Replacement of discretionary salt for people with \textbf{treated} hypertension$^{a,c}$
\end{enumerate}
\footnotesize
$^a$ Modeled BP-lowering benefits. $^b$ Includes hyperkalemia harms in CKD G3--G5. $^c$ Assumes clinical screening prevents use in 20\% of CKD G3--G5.

\medskip
\textbf{Working decision}: Focus on scenarios \textbf{4, 5} (discretionary-only). Pending confirmation.

## D. Front-of-Pack Labeling

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Packaged (no adjustment needed --- estimate already from packaged-food purchases).

\textbf{Selected study}: \textcite{taillie2024} --- Chile FOPWL, observed.

\textbf{Policy}: Mandatory black octagonal warning labels for Na, sugar, saturated fat, and calories. Includes school sales bans and marketing restrictions on labeled products.

\textbf{Population}: 2,844 urban Chilean households, 138,391 household-months, 13 of 16 regions. July 2013 -- June 2019.

\textbf{Effect size}: \textbf{--73.3 mg/capita/day (--13.8\%)} in sodium purchases.

\textbf{Caveat}: Purchases-to-intake translation is uncertain. Nadia's US/Canada work used purchases directly.

\textbf{Alternative}: Mexico 2026 study found --7\% (95\% CI --13\%, --2\%) in packaged-food/beverage \emph{sales} $\approx$ --38 mg/capita/day.

## E. Mandatory Salt Targets

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Packaged foods.

\textbf{Policy}: South African mandatory national sodium reduction legislation (2013); maximum sodium limits across 13 categories of processed foods; targets implemented 2016 and 2019.

\textbf{Selected study}: \textcite{strausskruger2022} --- African-PREDICT. $N=311$ healthy 20--30-year-olds, 24-hr urine. Baseline 2013--2017 vs.\ follow-up 2018--2020; mean follow-up 4.56 yrs.

\textbf{Effect size}: \textbf{--15.2\% sodium/day} (derived). Baseline/follow-up straddle target dates $\to$ likely \textbf{underestimates} true effect.

\textbf{Source adjustment}: ${\sim}$62\% of SA sodium from packaged food \autocite{charlton2005}. Raw adjustment yields 24.5\% reduction relative to packaged source; conservative estimate = 20\%.

\textbf{Alternative SA studies}: Gaziano 2025 (--8.4\%, rural, ${\geq}$40 yrs, spot urine) \autocite{gaziano2025}; Charlton 2021 (--18.4\%, national, methodological concerns) \autocite{charlton2021}.

\textbf{UK targets}: He 2013: --15\% over 7 yrs, voluntary \autocite{he2013}; Song 2023: --19.2\% over 11 yrs \autocite{song2023}.

\textbf{Mexico modeling}: Muci\~{n}o-Sandoval 2025: --25.2\% phase 1, --28.6\% phase 2 \autocite{mucinosandoval2025} --- justifies not using Gaziano's 8\%.

## F. Fiscal Policy / Taxation

\footnotesize

\textbf{Source targeted}: Packaged (no adjustment needed).

\textbf{Selected study}: \textcite{saxena2025} --- Philippines, modeled. Elasticity for food groups.

\textbf{Policy}: 20\% tax on foods high in salt and sugar; WHO WPRO nutrient-profile model; 100\% pass-through; industry reformulation (${\leq}$50\% above threshold).

\textbf{Population}: Adults of the Philippines, aged ${\geq}$25 years.

\textbf{Effect size}: \textbf{--100 mg Na/day (--10\%)} at year 20.

\textbf{Caveat}: High relative to other estimates; tax does not include fat.

\textbf{Alternative studies}:
\begin{itemize}
  \item India \autocite{roche2026}: --1.63\% over 30 yrs (40\% GST, non-standard tax structure).
  \item Australia \autocite{davies2026}: --110 mg/day ($\approx$ --3.22\%) over lifetime of current population.
  \item Australia \autocite{cobiac2017}: --67 mg/day under \$0.30/g Na excise.
  \item \textcite{dodd2020} systematic review: modeling studies predict 1--11\% decrease in salt intake.
\end{itemize}
